In the study of galaxy formation and evolution, the **energy loading factor** (often denoted as $\epsilon$ or $\alpha_E$) is a dimensionless parameter that quantifies the efficiency with which energy injected by astrophysical sources couples to the interstellar medium to drive large-scale [[galaxy-outflows|Galaxy outflows]]. Specifically, it is defined as the ratio of the outward kinetic and thermal energy flux carried by a galactic wind to the total energy injection rate provided by [[stellar-feedback-and-winds|Stellar Feedback and Winds]] or [[active-galactic-nuclei-agn-physics|Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) Physics]]. Alongside the closely related [[wind-mass-loading|Wind mass loading]] factor, the energy loading factor is a central component of the [[equilibrium-recycling-model|Equilibrium recycling model]] of the cosmic baryon cycle [Davé et al. (2011)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2012MNRAS.421...98D/abstract). By dictating how much of the raw feedback energy is successfully thermalized and retained to perform mechanical work against the host galaxy's gravitational potential, this parameter determines a galaxy's ability to drive outflows, halt runaway gas cooling, and regulate its ongoing [[average-star-formation-efficiency|star formation]]. 

The physical mechanisms governing energy loading depend strongly on the depth of the galaxy's gravitational well. In low-mass galaxies, the energy budget is dominated by core-collapse supernovae and massive stellar winds, which can generate highly pressurized thermal bubbles that drive continuous [[superwinds|Superwinds]]. Observational benchmarks, such as the archetypal starburst galaxy M82, demonstrate that the thermalization efficiency of supernova energy can be remarkably high, successfully coupling $30\%$ to $100\%$ of the injected energy into the hot wind fluid [Strickland et al. (2009)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2009ApJ...697.2030S/abstract). Above the [[transition-halo-mass-scale|Transition Halo Mass Scale]] of approximately $10^{12} M_\odot$, the deepening gravitational potential renders stellar feedback insufficient to loft material into the circumgalactic medium. In this regime, AGN-driven [[mechanical-feedback|Mechanical feedback]]—particularly via relativistic jets—becomes the primary regulator of the galactic environment [Fabian et al. (2012)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2012ARA&A..50..455F/abstract). Interestingly, while the mass loading factor is widely observed to scale inversely with galaxy mass, theoretical models suggest the energy loading factor remains relatively invariant across a broad range of halo masses and redshifts.

Because cosmological hydrodynamical simulations lack the spatial resolution to capture the exact microphysics of supernovae and black hole accretion, the energy loading factor serves as a highly calibrated input within [[subgrid-physics-prescriptions|Subgrid physics prescriptions]] to successfully reproduce the observed galaxy mass function. However, the theoretical reliance on highly efficient energy loading to quench low-mass galaxies currently faces severe observational tensions. While simulations often require extreme loading factors to match cosmic abundances, recent local observations of dwarf starbursts reveal a much gentler baryon cycle, yielding empirical mass and energy loading efficiencies orders of magnitude lower than predicted. Resolving this discrepancy requires untangling the complex thermodynamics of the [[multiphase-wind|Multiphase wind]], addressing systematic offsets between emission and absorption line diagnostics, and incorporating high-redshift insights from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). These early-universe observations suggest that highly efficient energy loading at cosmic dawn may have initially driven an epoch of [[positive-feedback-astrophysics|Positive feedback (astrophysics)]]—stimulating star formation via pressurized turbulence—prior to the onset of the energy-conserving quenching phase that dominates the local universe.

## Definition and Physical Significance

The energy loading factor, typically denoted as $\epsilon$ or $\alpha_E$, is a fundamental dimensionless parameter in models of galaxy formation and evolution. It is defined as the ratio of the energy flux carried by a galactic outflow to the total energy injection rate provided by astrophysical sources. Mathematically, it is expressed as:
$$ \epsilon = \frac{\dot{E}_{\mathrm{out}}}{\dot{E}_{\mathrm{inj}}} $$
where $\dot{E}_{\mathrm{out}}$ encompasses the outward [[wind-mechanical-energy|kinetic and thermal energy flux]] of the ejected gas, and $\dot{E}_{\mathrm{inj}}$ represents the total mechanical or radiative power supplied by [[stellar-feedback-and-winds|Stellar Feedback and Winds]] or [[active-galactic-nuclei-agn-physics|Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) Physics]]. This parameter serves as a direct quantitative measure of the thermalization efficiency and the overall coupling efficiency of feedback energy to the interstellar medium.

**Stellar Feedback Constraints**
The energetics of these outflows are fundamentally rooted in high-energy processes including synchrotron radiation, cosmic ray acceleration, and plasma dynamics within the interstellar medium [Longair et al. (2011)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2011hea..book.....L/abstract). Foundational studies of interstellar dynamics identify supernovae and the expansion of gas around young O stars as the primary sources of kinetic energy driving the gas cycle [Spitzer et al. (1968)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1968nim..book....1S/abstract). Early galaxy energy budget analyses utilized infrared emission and CO surveys to link the interstellar energy density to the large-scale distribution of molecular clouds [Puget et al. (1985)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1985bis..conf...77P/abstract). 

In star-forming galaxies today, energy is injected primarily by supernovae and massive stellar winds. The physical significance of $\epsilon$ lies in its determination of whether these energy inputs can successfully heat the interstellar medium, overcome radiative losses, and drive large-scale [[superwinds|Superwinds]]. Direct empirical constraints on the energy loading factor are challenging to obtain, but detailed multi-wavelength observations of local starbursts provide critical benchmarks. For example, hydrodynamical modeling of the hot X-ray emitting plasma in M82 restricts the energy loading factor to $0.3 \le \epsilon \le 1.0$ [Strickland et al. (2009)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2009ApJ...697.2030S/abstract). Interestingly, while the mass loading factor of [[galaxy-outflows|Galaxy outflows]] is consistently observed and simulated to scale inversely with halo mass, the energy loading factor associated with stellar feedback appears to be nearly independent of both halo mass and redshift in modern cosmological simulations [Oren et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv251023343O/abstract).

**AGN Feedback and Kinetic Coupling**
In massive galaxies, where the gravitational potential is deep, AGN feedback becomes the dominant regulatory mechanism. In this regime, the energy loading factor—often termed the kinetic coupling efficiency—dictates the fraction of the accreted rest-mass energy or AGN bolometric luminosity that is converted into the [[kinetic-power|Kinetic Power]] of jets and wide-angle outflows. Measuring this efficiency observationally is fraught with systematic uncertainty; deriving kinetic coupling efficiencies from typical optical or molecular outflow signatures requires geometric and timescale assumptions that often do not align with simulated feedback models [Harrison et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018NatAs...2..198H/abstract). Independent constraints on the baryon energy loading efficiency of AGN jets, derived from the diffuse gamma-ray and neutrino flux limits of galaxy clusters (e.g., the Coma cluster), suggest that this coupling is highly inefficient on macro scales, yielding firm upper limits of $\eta < 0.1$ and potentially as low as $\eta \lesssim 2 \times 10^{-3}$ [Shi et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2022ApJ...927...33S/abstract), [Shi et al. (2023)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023ApJ...957..101S/abstract).

**Thermodynamic Balance and Self-Regulation**
The physical significance of the energy loading factor extends beyond the simple ejection of gas. In equilibrium models of galactic atmospheres, the balance between radiative cooling and feedback heating determines whether the circumgalactic medium contracts or expands. A high coupling efficiency ensures sufficient energy is available to resist atmospheric contraction. Paradoxically, if a galaxy experiences high mass loading, it may require a proportionately larger energy injection to offset the gravitational work required to lift the material; in such cases, galaxies might reach higher [[equilibrium-star-formation-rates|Equilibrium star formation rates]] simply to supply the necessary energy flux [Voit et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024arXiv240607631V/abstract). Consequently, accurately modeling the energy loading factor is essential for understanding the self-regulation of baryon cycles across cosmic time.

## Historical Development of Feedback Models

The theoretical foundation for the energy loading factor and [[wind-mass-loading|Wind mass loading]] originated in early analytic efforts to understand the chemical evolution and gas retention of galaxies. The genesis of modern galactic wind theory can be traced to the realization that the interstellar medium (ISM) could be heavily influenced by the [[kinetic-power|Kinetic Power]] injected by supernova explosions. As first postulated by Mathews & Baker (1971), the ISM of an elliptical galaxy can be heated by supernovae until the thermal energy of the gas exceeds the local gravitational binding energy, driving a large-scale outflow. 

Expanding upon this energetic threshold, Larson (1974) noted that the binding energy per unit gas mass is inherently higher in more massive galaxies. Consequently, massive systems can retain their gas against supernova-driven expansion for longer periods, naturally attaining higher average [[metallicity-distributions-and-scaling-relations|stellar metallicities]] before the gas is expelled. Combined with the prevailing assumption of monolithic collapse, this classic ejective wind model successfully explained the observed correlation between a galaxy's metallicity and velocity dispersion. 

In these foundational frameworks, feedback was largely treated as a catastrophic, terminal event—often referred to as strong [[negative-feedback|Negative feedback]]—that permanently evacuated gas from the galactic potential well. The energy loading factor, in this early context, was implicitly treated as a threshold parameter: once the integrated mechanical energy from [[stellar-feedback-and-winds|Stellar Feedback and Winds]] or [[active-galactic-nuclei-agn-physics|Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) Physics]] surpassed the binding energy, star formation ceased. 

However, as cosmological hydrodynamical simulations and spatially resolved observations advanced, it became clear that a purely ejective model was insufficient to capture the full baryon cycle. Early hydrodynamical simulations demonstrated that kinetic energy feedback could successfully transport heavy elements into the intergalactic medium, efficiently enriching the gas out to distances of several hundred kiloparsecs [Steinmetz et al. (1997)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1997seim.proc..281S/abstract). Not all gas escapes the dark matter halo; a significant fraction (roughly $50\%$) of outflowing gas is recycled and reaccreted on timescales of $\sim 1$ Gyr [Christensen et al. (2015)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2016ApJ...824...57C/abstract). This realization prompted a major paradigm shift from terminal ejection to the [[equilibrium-recycling-model|Equilibrium recycling model]] of galaxy evolution [Davé et al. (2011)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2012MNRAS.421...98D/abstract). In this modern framework, galaxies are posited to exist in a slowly evolving, self-regulated state where [[net-gas-inflows|Net gas inflows]], star formation, and feedback-driven outflows balance one another.

Within the equilibrium model, the mass and energy loading factors are the central parameters defining the efficiency of this self-regulation. The mass loading factor, typically denoted $\beta$ (or $\eta$), is defined as the ratio of the mass outflow rate to the star formation rate:
$$ \beta = \frac{\dot{M}_{\rm out}}{\dot{M}_*} $$
Rather than acting as a singular off-switch, feedback regulates star formation continuously. Modern scaling relations typically parametrize the mass loading factor as an inverse function of the circular velocity, $\beta \propto v_{\rm circ}^{-\alpha}$ (with $\alpha$ often between $1.5$ and $2.2$), reflecting the differential efficiency of feedback in shallow versus deep potential wells [Mitchell et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020MNRAS.494.3971M/abstract). 

Despite the success of the equilibrium framework, the precise energy and mass loading efficiencies required to balance this cycle remain a subject of active debate. As observational capabilities have improved, the tension between the violent, highly loaded outflows required by theory and the gentler baryon cycles observed in nearby dwarf galaxies has highlighted the ongoing evolution of feedback models, pushing the field from simple analytic thresholds toward highly complex [[multi-scale-feedback-processes|Multi-scale feedback processes]].

## Drivers of Energy Injection: Stellar vs. AGN

The mechanisms responsible for energy injection into galactic environments transition sharply as a function of halo mass. In low-mass systems, the energy budget is governed by [[stellar-feedback-and-winds|Stellar Feedback and Winds]], primarily through supernova explosions and stellar winds. Conversely, in massive galaxies and clusters—typically above a halo mass scale of $10^{12} M_\odot$—the injection of energy is dominated by [[active-galactic-nuclei-agn-physics|Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) Physics]] [Fabian et al. (2012)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2012ARA&A..50..455F/abstract), [Mitchell et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020MNRAS.494.3971M/abstract).

**Stellar Feedback in Low-Mass Halos**
In the dwarf and spiral galaxy regimes, the dominant source of [[kinetic-power|Kinetic Power]] and thermal heating is stellar feedback. Studies of supernova parent galaxies indicate that Type II and Ib supernovae are associated with the cooler component of far-infrared radiation, implying their progenitors are typically in the $5-10\ M_\odot$ range [Petrosyan et al. (1992)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1992A&A...261..433P/abstract). Core-collapse supernova feedback and winds from massive young stellar objects thermalize their ejecta, creating high-pressure bubbles that drive [[superwinds|Superwinds]]. The resulting plasma can reach temperatures of tens of millions of Kelvin and terminal velocities significantly exceeding the galactic escape velocity [Strickland et al. (2009)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2009ApJ...697.2030S/abstract).

Beyond isolated star formation, galaxy interactions and mergers produce [[galactic-torques|strong torques]] that drive radial gas flows, potentially flattening [[abundance-gradients|abundance gradients]] and enhancing central star formation, which complicates the loading efficiency of the resulting starburst [Combes et al. (1997)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1998ASPC..147..300C/abstract). In starbursting mergers, the scaling laws for star formation are non-universal, as gas turbulence and fragmentation can drive extended star formation in massive clusters, altering the available energy budget [Bournaud et al. (2011)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2011EAS....51..107B/abstract).

The efficiency with which this energy couples to the ISM to drive mass out of the potential well generally scales inversely with the circular velocity $v_{\rm circ}$ of the halo:
$$ \beta \propto v_{\rm circ}^{-\alpha} $$
where $\alpha$ is typically between $1.5$ and $2.2$ [Christensen et al. (2015)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2016ApJ...824...57C/abstract), [Mitchell et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020MNRAS.494.3971M/abstract). However, there is a prominent unresolved tension in the literature regarding the exact magnitude of this coupling. Cosmological simulations rely on highly efficient feedback models, requiring mass loading factors of $\beta \sim 1 - 50$ to reproduce the low-mass end of the stellar mass function [Christensen et al. (2015)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2016ApJ...824...57C/abstract), [Mitchell et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020MNRAS.494.3971M/abstract). In contrast, a growing body of local empirical observations finds much gentler baryon cycles, with mass loading factors frequently estimated to be near-unity or lower [Marasco et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023A&A...670A..92M/abstract), [Kado-Fong et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024ApJ...966..129K/abstract). 

**AGN Feedback in Massive Halos**
As galaxies grow and their deep gravitational potentials render stellar feedback inefficient at driving halo-scale outflows, supermassive black holes become the primary engines of energy loading. AGN feedback operates broadly in two regimes: a radiative mode (often modeled as a thermal mode) and a kinetic mode [Fabian et al. (2012)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2012ARA&A..50..455F/abstract), [Oren et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv251023343O/abstract).

The radiative mode is dominant during high-luminosity accretion phases, driving thermal winds that can clear the central gas reservoirs. Meanwhile, the kinetic mode is characterized by highly collimated AGN jets that inject copious mechanical energy into the surrounding medium. This [[mechanical-feedback|Mechanical feedback]] is essential for maintaining a long-lived heating and cooling balance within [[intracluster-and-intragroup-phenomena|Intracluster and Intragroup Phenomena]], preventing catastrophic gas cooling [Fabian et al. (2012)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2012ARA&A..50..455F/abstract). While cosmological simulations note that the suppression of the power spectrum of local gas density fields on gigaparsec scales is primarily a consequence of star formation depleting gas, the impact of AGN feedback is restricted to smaller scales ($k > 0.1 \ h/\rm Mpc$) [Ondaro-Mallea et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024arXiv241209526O/abstract). Nevertheless, AGN jets are capable of driving massive gas outflows when the jets undergo precession [Kader et al. (2026)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2026arXiv260108791K/abstract).

**Cosmic Evolution of Energy Drivers**
The relative influence of stellar and AGN drivers evolves across cosmic time. While star formation-driven outflows dominate low-mass galaxies at all epochs, jet heating represents the primary growth impediment for massive galaxies in the local universe. Interestingly, at cosmic noon ($z = 1-3$), the outflow budgets from star formation, radiative AGN winds, and kinetic jet heating are roughly equal [Buchner et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024A&A...689L...2B/abstract). Furthermore, while contemporary models view feedback as a primarily [[negative-feedback|Negative feedback]] process that quenches star formation, recent high-redshift observations suggest an early epoch ($z > 6$) where energy injection drove radiatively cooled turbulence that stimulated early star formation (a form of [[positive-feedback-astrophysics|Positive feedback (astrophysics)]]) before transitioning to the modern, energy-conserving quenching regime [Silk et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024ApJ...961L..39S/abstract). Notably, while mass loading is strongly mass-dependent, some cosmological simulations suggest that the overall *energy* loading factors may remain remarkably uniform across both mass and redshift scales, reflecting a universal self-regulation in the cosmic baryon cycle [Oren et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv251023343O/abstract).

## Observational Diagnostics and Estimation

Quantifying the energy and mass loading factors of galactic outflows requires multi-wavelength observations that can trace the kinematics and thermodynamics of the multi-phase interstellar and circumgalactic medium. The fundamental galactic parameters used to compute loading factors, such as stellar mass and star-formation history, are primarily extracted via stellar population synthesis modeling of panchromatic spectral energy distributions (SEDs) [Conroy et al. (2013)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2013ARA&A..51..393C/abstract). A galaxy's SED acts as a fingerprint that allows researchers to reconstruct the evolutionary history and physical processes regulating its mass and energy loading [Iyer et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv250217680I/abstract). Because outflows consist of hot plasma, warm ionized and neutral gas, and cold molecular material, inferring the total [[kinetic-power|Kinetic Power]] and outflow rates relies heavily on calibrating phase-specific diagnostics and understanding their underlying systematic biases.

The primary energy reservoir of a stellar or AGN-driven wind is often the hot, tenuous plasma. Measurements of hard X-ray emission provide critical constraints on the thermalization efficiency and the central mass loading of this phase. For example, X-ray constraints in the local starburst M82 indicate high thermalization efficiencies ($\epsilon \sim 30-100\%$) and mild mass loading factors ($\beta \sim 1.0-2.8$) for the hot fluid, which reaches temperatures of $30-80 \times 10^6$ K [Strickland et al. (2009)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2009ApJ...697.2030S/abstract). Theoretical estimates of the hot gas filling factor in our Milky Way suggest it occupies a small fraction ($\sim 20\%$) of the interstellar volume at the solar circle, primarily concentrated at low altitudes [Ferrière et al. (1998)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1998ApJ...503..700F/abstract). While optical and sub-millimeter observations trace the cooler, entrained "sparks" of the outflow, future instruments such as an X-ray microcalorimeter are required to directly map the bulk energy carried by the hot wind fluid [Tremblay et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2019BAAS...51c.480T/abstract).

The warm ionized and neutral gas phases are typically traced via UV and optical absorption and emission lines to determine the outflow velocity and [[ionised-mass-outflow-rate|Ionised Mass Outflow Rate]]. However, a significant systematic tension exists between these two diagnostics. Because emission line luminosity is proportional to the square of the gas density, whereas absorption line profiles scale linearly with column density, emission-derived outflow properties consistently underestimate the true outflow kinematics. Maximum outflow velocities and line widths derived from emission lines reach only 60-70% of those measured from absorption lines, yielding mass outflow rates that are systematically lower by $0.2-0.5$ dex [Xu et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025ApJ...984...94X/abstract). Despite these diagnostic tensions, biconical outflows of multiphase gas oriented perpendicular to galaxy disks have been established as a robust descriptor for star-formation-driven winds throughout the second half of cosmic history [Rupke et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018Galax...6..138R/abstract).

Observational estimates of the mass loading factor heavily contextualize theoretical efficiencies. Resolved absorption-line studies in lensed galaxies at $z=1.87$ measure mass loading factors of $\log \eta = 0.04 \pm 0.34$ for the low-ionization phase [Vasan et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025ApJ...981..105V/abstract). Similarly, differential modeling of low-redshift galaxy populations finds a near-unity total [[wind-mass-loading|mass loading factor]] ($\eta_{\rm m} = 0.92_{-0.74}^{+1.76}$) [Kado-Fong et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024ApJ...966..129K/abstract), and integral field spectroscopy of local dwarf starbursts reveals gentle gas cycles with loading factors as low as $\beta \simeq 0.02$ [Marasco et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023A&A...670A..92M/abstract). 

To quantify [[molecular-outflows|Molecular outflows]] and their contribution to mass loading, researchers map CO and dust emission. A major uncertainty in converting CO luminosities to total H$_2$ mass is the CO-to-H$_2$ conversion factor. Analytic formulae have been developed to calibrate the conversion factor as a function of galactic metallicity and absolute magnitude, reflecting its radial dependence within disks [Arimoto et al. (1996)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1996PASJ...48..275A/abstract). In galaxies like M51, the conversion factor is found to be lower than the Galactic mean in spiral arms but increases significantly in the outer disk where CO intensities are low [Nakai et al. (1995)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1995PASJ...47..761N/abstract). This factor is not universal and increases rapidly as metallicity decreases, reaching values at least 10 times the Galactic standard in low-metallicity dwarf galaxies [Wilson et al. (1995)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1995ApJ...448L..97W/abstract), [Komugi et al. (2011)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2011PASJ...63L...1K/abstract), and observations of extremely metal-poor galaxies like GR 8 suggest it can reach values at least 80 times the Galactic standard in the vicinity of star-forming regions [Verter et al. (1995)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1995ApJ...446..616V/abstract). Recent studies also suggest that the dust-to-metals ratio (D/M) varies across galactic environments and is sensitive to the choice of CO-to-H$_2$ conversion factor, particularly in dense central regions [Chiang et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021ApJ...907...29C/abstract). While the dense gas tracer HCN exhibits a strong metallicity-dependent conversion factor, others such as HCO$^+$ appear much less sensitive to metallicity [Patra et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025ApJ...983..133P/abstract), complicating the accurate measurement of cold gas expulsion in metal-poor environments.

Finally, in the context of [[active-galactic-nuclei-agn-physics|Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) Physics]], estimating the kinetic coupling efficiency requires relating the outflow's kinetic power to the bolometric AGN luminosity. This process relies on numerous dynamic and geometric assumptions, including the calibration of the virial factor used to determine the mass of the central black hole from broad-line region gas [Park et al. (2012)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2012ApJS..203....6P/abstract). For AGN feedback, the observed infrared properties may also be influenced by a hot dust covering factor that decreases as the AGN luminosity increases, impacting kinetic power estimates [Son et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2022ApJ...927..107S/abstract). Due to these uncertainties, researchers caution against directly comparing observationally derived kinetic coupling efficiencies to the parameters used in idealized [[stellar-and-agn-feedback|Stellar and AGN Feedback]] models [Harrison et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018NatAs...2..198H/abstract).

## Scaling Relations with Galaxy and Halo Mass

The energetics of [[galaxy-outflows|Galaxy outflows]] are fundamentally tied to the depth of the host galaxy's gravitational potential. However, the efficiency with which feedback mass and energy couple to the interstellar and circumgalactic medium scale differently with galaxy size. While the [[wind-mass-loading|Wind mass loading]] factor (often denoted as $\eta_m$ or $\beta$) exhibits a strong inverse dependence on galaxy mass, the energy loading factor remains notably invariant across a wide range of halo masses.

In the low-mass regime where [[stellar-feedback-and-winds|Stellar Feedback and Winds]] dominate, the binding energy per unit gas mass is relatively small. Supernova explosions and stellar winds easily heat the interstellar medium beyond its gravitational binding energy, driving extensive mass loss and leading to poor baryon retention in dwarf galaxies [Yu et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv251205584Y/abstract). Consequently, cosmological simulations consistently predict a steep inverse $v_{\rm circ}$ scaling for the mass loading factor. High-resolution zoom-in simulations and large-volume models find that mass loading scales with circular velocity as roughly $v_{\rm circ}^{-1.5}$ to $v_{\rm circ}^{-2.2}$ [Christensen et al. (2015)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2016ApJ...824...57C/abstract), [Mitchell et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020MNRAS.494.3971M/abstract). 

In stark contrast to mass loading, the energy loading factor—the fraction of available stellar feedback energy that is successfully retained as kinetic or thermal energy in the wind—appears relatively constant. Analyses of cosmological simulations demonstrate that while wind mass loadings decrease significantly with increasing halo virial mass and redshift, energy loadings are nearly independent of both parameters [Oren et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv251023343O/abstract). This theoretical invariance is consistent with analytic models for energy-driven winds that rely purely on the halo potential, where a constant fraction of supernova energy is successfully coupled to the outflow regardless of how much total mass is entrained [Christensen et al. (2015)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2016ApJ...824...57C/abstract). 

These scaling relations undergo a fundamental shift at the [[transition-halo-mass-scale|Transition Halo Mass Scale]] of $\sim 10^{12} M_\odot$. Above this threshold, stellar feedback becomes insufficient to regulate the massive circumgalactic atmosphere, and [[active-galactic-nuclei-agn-physics|Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) Physics]] becomes the dominant feedback mechanism. In this high-mass regime, the mass loading factor ceases its inverse scaling and exhibits an upturn driven by AGN kinetic and thermal modes [Mitchell et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020MNRAS.494.3971M/abstract). 

**Observational Tensions**
As noted in prior sections, the literature exhibits a severe discrepancy regarding the scaling and magnitude of these feedback efficiencies in low-mass galaxies. To reproduce the observed stellar mass function, cosmological simulations require extreme mass loading in dwarf galaxies ($\eta_m \sim 1-50$). However, empirical constraints robustly contradict these high values, finding $\eta_m$ ranging from $\sim 0.92$ down to $\sim 0.02$ [Kado-Fong et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024ApJ...966..129K/abstract), [Marasco et al. (2023)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023A&A...670A..92M/abstract). Complicating this theoretical picture, analytic frameworks evaluating galactic atmospheric equilibrium suggest that scaling relations are highly interdependent; artificially increasing the mass loading factor in models can actually result in *higher* equilibrium star formation rates, disrupting conventional scaling assumptions [Voit et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024arXiv240607631V/abstract).

## The Role of Energy Loading in the Baryon Cycle

The energy loading factor is a fundamental parameter in [[self-regulated-feedback-mechanisms|Self-regulated feedback mechanisms]], dictating how efficiently mechanical energy from [[stellar-feedback-and-winds|Stellar Feedback and Winds]] and active galactic nuclei couples to the interstellar medium (ISM) and circumgalactic medium (CGM). In the context of the cosmic baryon cycle, galaxies are often modeled as existing in a slowly evolving equilibrium between cosmological gas inflow, star formation, and feedback-driven outflows [Davé et al. (2011)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2012MNRAS.421...98D/abstract). Efficient energy loading regulates the star formation rate by heating the surrounding gas and driving [[galaxy-and-gaseous-outflows|Galaxy and gaseous outflows]], thereby maintaining a delicate balance against the galactic gas cooling rate.

Measurements of H$\alpha$ emission in galactic halos indicate that the mass cooling rate of the CGM routinely exceeds the central star formation rate by factors of $4$ to $90$ [Zhang et al. (2021)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021ApJ...916..101Z/abstract). Consequently, efficient energy loading provides crucial preventative feedback, halting runaway cooling and avoiding the over-accumulation of cold gas in the ISM. However, the theoretical literature presents a nuanced view of how energy and mass loading interact to regulate the CGM. While traditional models assume that a high mass loading factor strictly suppresses star formation, recent analyses of the equilibrium states of galactic atmospheres suggest the opposite can occur: increasing the mass loading can paradoxically require a higher equilibrium star formation rate, as a larger continuous energy injection is needed to support the CGM against gravitational contraction when the outflowing mass burden is high [Voit et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024arXiv240607631V/abstract).

A critical consequence of energy-loaded outflows is large-scale gas recycling. Outflows enrich the CGM with dust and metals, which in turn alters the local cooling function. To observationally constrain the magnitude of mass loss and the effective metal loading factor, researchers frequently utilize the "oxygen deficit" observed in local star-forming galaxies, which quantifies the heavy elements missing from the ISM due to outflow expulsion [Zahid et al. (2013)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2014Ap&SS.349..873Z/abstract). Because metal-enriched gas has a higher cooling rate, it is highly susceptible to reaccretion. Cosmological zoom simulations demonstrate that approximately $50\%$ of the ejected outflow mass is ultimately reaccreted onto the galaxy on timescales of $\sim 1 \text{ Gyr}$ [Christensen et al. (2015)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2016ApJ...824...57C/abstract), [van de Voort et al. (2016)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2017ASSL..430..301V/abstract). Observational constraints of lensed star-forming galaxies at cosmic noon support this [[equilibrium-recycling-model|Equilibrium recycling model]]: the bulk of the outflowing low-ionization gas often travels at speeds below the halo escape velocity [Vasan et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025ApJ...981..105V/abstract). Thus, rather than permanently expelling gas into the intergalactic medium, continuous energy loading frequently lofts material into the inner CGM, establishing a circulating, metal-rich gas reservoir that sustains future star formation.

## Numerical Simulations and Subgrid Prescriptions

In models of galaxy formation, numerical simulations of cosmological hydrodynamics lack the spatial resolution to capture the exact microphysics of supernovae and black hole accretion. Consequently, they must rely on [[subgrid-physics-prescriptions|Subgrid physics prescriptions]] to inject momentum and thermal energy into the interstellar medium. The energy loading factor, alongside the mass loading factor, is a fundamental parameter in these models, heavily calibrated to reproduce macroscopic observables such as the galaxy stellar mass function.

In the low-mass galaxy regime, [[stellar-feedback-and-winds|Stellar Feedback and Winds]] dictate the baryon cycle. Simulations consistently model this by scaling the feedback loading factors with the depth of the gravitational potential. For example, modern cosmological models typically apply a dimensionless mass loading factor that scales with circular velocity as roughly $v_{\rm circ}^{-1.5}$ to $v_{\rm circ}^{-2.2}$ [Mitchell et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020MNRAS.494.3971M/abstract), [Christensen et al. (2015)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2016ApJ...824...57C/abstract). By contrast, the corresponding energy loading factors injected into the simulated gas remain rigidly independent of both mass and redshift [Oren et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv251023343O/abstract). 

The values of these subgrid parameters remain a subject of active debate, as cosmological models exhibit a severe discrepancy with empirical data. To sufficiently quench low-mass halos and match cosmic abundances, simulations typically require mass loading factors ($\beta \sim 1-50$) that far exceed those observationally derived from local starburst dwarf galaxies [Kado-Fong et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024ApJ...966..129K/abstract), [Marasco et al. (2023)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023A&A...670A..92M/abstract). This implies that actual stellar feedback may drive a far gentler cycle than subgrid physics models currently implement.

In massive halos ($M > 10^{12} M_\odot$), [[active-galactic-nuclei-agn-physics|Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) Physics]] become the dominant regulatory mechanism, causing a sharp upturn in the mass loading factor [Mitchell et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020MNRAS.494.3971M/abstract). Subgrid models for AGN feedback often parameterize this energy injection via a kinetic coupling efficiency, which defines the fraction of the accreted AGN bolometric luminosity that is mechanically coupled to the surrounding gas as jet or wind power. However, linking the kinetic coupling efficiency in fiducial simulations to physical reality remains highly problematic. The observationally derived coupling efficiencies rely on heavily idealized assumptions regarding outflow geometry, density, and timescale. Consequently, extreme caution must be exercised when comparing empirical measurements of AGN outflow power directly to the kinetic coupling efficiencies encoded in subgrid simulation models [Harrison et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018NatAs...2..198H/abstract), [Harrison et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024IAUS..378...57H/abstract).

## High-Redshift Evolution and JWST Insights

Recent observations of the early universe, particularly those enabled by JWST, suggest a paradigm shift in our understanding of feedback energetics and the energy loading factor during the cosmic dawn. Standard theoretical frameworks and [[subgrid-physics-prescriptions|Subgrid physics prescriptions]] often characterize galactic feedback as primarily a quenching mechanism ([[negative-feedback|Negative feedback]]). However, recent insights indicate a strong redshift evolution in how injected energy couples to the interstellar medium. 

At $z > 6$, feedback is thought to be dominated by a short-lived "[[positive-feedback-astrophysics|Positive feedback (astrophysics)]]" phase [Silk et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024ApJ...961L..39S/abstract). In this early regime, momentum-conserving outflows and AGN-driven radiatively cooled turbulence compress dense gas and stimulate vigorous star formation, rather than solely expelling it. The signature of this turbulent dissipation in high-redshift galaxies is frequently revealed by unusually powerful H$_2$ line emission, highlighting warm molecular hydrogen as a key cooling agent in these chaotic early environments [Guillard et al. (2015)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2015sf2a.conf...81G/abstract). This helps resolve tensions in standard stellar feedback models, which struggle to reproduce the observed star formation rates in gas-rich, high-redshift galaxies without invoking additional structural support, such as large-scale turbulent driving parallel to the galactic disk, to regulate the gas to the [[kennicutt-schmidt-law|Kennicutt-Schmidt law]] [Brucy et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020ApJ...896L..34B/abstract). Around $z \sim 6$, a transition appears to occur independently of galaxy mass. The feedback regime shifts toward late-stage, energy-conserving outflows that efficiently heat and deplete circumgalactic gas reservoirs, transitioning the host galaxies into a quenching phase [Silk et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024ApJ...961L..39S/abstract).

The redshift evolution of the energy loading factor also profoundly influences the Lyman continuum escape fraction ($f_{\rm esc}$), a critical parameter for cosmic reionization. High energy loading in early galaxies drives powerful outflows that carve low-density channels through the ISM, allowing ionizing radiation to leak into the intergalactic medium. Theoretical models predict that radiation-driven outflows develop efficiently once a galaxy's specific star formation rate exceeds a critical threshold of ${\rm sSFR}^* \approx 25\ {\rm Gyr}^{-1}$ [Ferrara et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv250510619F/abstract). As the average specific star formation rate increases with redshift, the globally averaged [[photon-escape-fraction|escape fraction]] is predicted to rise dramatically from $0.007$ in the local universe to approximately $0.6$ at $z \approx 20$ [Ferrara et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv250510619F/abstract).

Such high escape values are observationally necessary to balance the reionization budget. Recent analyses of the mean free path of ionizing photons at $z \sim 6$ imply a high intergalactic clumping factor of $C \approx 12$ [Davies et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024arXiv240618186D/abstract). Overcoming this recombination sink requires early galaxies to produce roughly twice as many ionizing photons ($\approx 3$ photons per baryon) as traditionally assumed [Davies et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024arXiv240618186D/abstract). Highly efficient, outflow-boosted escape fractions help reconcile the required reionization history with the exceptionally luminous early galaxy populations revealed by JWST.

While direct constraints on the kinetic energy loading of these early winds are challenging to obtain, specialized observations are beginning to map their kinematics. For instance, observations of dusty star-forming galaxies at $z=5.3$ have resolved fast [[molecular-outflows|Molecular outflows]] reaching velocities up to $800\ {\rm km\ s}^{-1}$ [Spilker et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018Sci...361.1016S/abstract). These early molecular winds exhibit mass-loading factors near unity, demonstrating that even within the first billion years of cosmic history, feedback was already capable of injecting substantial kinetic energy and removing a large fraction of the gas available for future star formation. At slightly lower redshifts ($z \sim 3$), massive galaxies are observed to drive exceptionally high-velocity outflows, reaching speeds up to $1500\ {\rm km\ s}^{-1}$, which are often associated with concurrent AGN activity rather than typical Lyman-break galaxy star formation [Karman et al. (2013)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2014A&A...565A...5K/abstract).

## Open Questions and Future Directions

Significant uncertainties remain in quantifying the energy loading factor of galactic outflows, driven largely by the complex, [[multiphase-wind|Multiphase wind]] structure of these systems [Zhang et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018Galax...6..114Z/abstract). A primary open question concerns the systematic discrepancies between outflow properties derived from different observational tracers. Recent studies comparing UV absorption and optical emission lines reveal that mass outflow rates derived from emission lines are consistently $0.2$ to $0.5$ dex lower than those inferred from absorption [Xu et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025ApJ...984...94X/abstract). Furthermore, the maximum velocities and line widths measured in emission typically reach only $60\%$ to $70\%$ of their absorption-line counterparts [Xu et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025ApJ...984...94X/abstract). This tension likely arises from the varying density sensitivities of the diagnostics: emission line luminosities scale with the square of the local gas density, thus emphasizing denser, slower clumps, while absorption depths scale linearly with column density. Reconciling these density-weighted kinematic offsets is crucial for accurately constraining the true kinetic energy flux.

The physical state of the outflowing gas presents an additional theoretical challenge, particularly regarding nonequilibrium ionization. Calculations of mass and energy loading routinely rely on column density measurements of highly ionized species such as O VI and N V, which are conventionally interpreted assuming the gas is in photoionization equilibrium. However, hydrodynamic models demonstrate that the atomic ionization structure within steady-state outflows departs strongly from equilibrium [Gray et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2019ApJ...875..110G/abstract). Failing to account for this nonequilibrium chemistry leads to misinterpretations of the local radiation field and the total mass of the hot gas phase, thereby skewing the derived thermal and kinetic energy budgets.

Another dimension of complexity involves the transport of heavy elements and the efficiency of dust entrainment. Cosmological simulations indicate that the cold, dense phase of a galactic wind is significantly more dust-enriched than the hot, tenuous, volume-filling medium [Kannan et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021MNRAS.503..336K/abstract). Tracking the energy required to lift this multiphase material into the circumgalactic medium requires a precise understanding of the outflow geometry. Galactic winds are highly structured and typically manifest as anisotropic outflows aligned along the [[minor-axis-outflows|Minor-axis outflows]] of the galaxy [Mitchell et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020MNRAS.494.3971M/abstract). Observations of velocity-dependent covering fractions further confirm that outflowing gas is patchy [Vasan et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025ApJ...981..105V/abstract), which complicates the geometric and solid-angle assumptions required to translate line-of-sight velocities into global energy loading factors. Furthermore, the morphology and clumpiness of the interstellar medium play a crucial role in starlight attenuation, requiring complex models of dust evolution to accurately interpret the spectral energy distribution and multi-wavelength energy content of these outflows [Dwek et al. (2000)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2000LNP...548..157D/abstract).

Finally, the extent to which cosmic rays contribute to the total energy loading remains a dynamic area of research. While cosmic ray pressure is recognized as a potentially vital launching mechanism alongside thermal and [[radiation-pressure|Radiation pressure]] [Zhang et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018Galax...6..114Z/abstract), its specific coupling efficiency is poorly constrained. In massive halos governed by [[active-galactic-nuclei-agn-physics|Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) Physics]], the baryon loading factor of relativistic AGN jets—defined as the efficiency with which gravitational energy is converted into relativistic cosmic ray protons—is similarly uncertain. Future observational facilities and sophisticated [[multi-scale-multi-science-systems|Multi-scale multi-science systems]] will be necessary to resolve these tensions and fully map the energetics of the cosmic baryon cycle.
